reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Walsh and Hoyt's Clinical Neuro-Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Acellular calcified deposits within the optic nerve head that are usually bilateral and often an incidental finding
The central clinical importance is that they cause pseudopapilloedema, mimicking true disc swelling and prompting unnecessary investigation if not recognised
Superficial drusen appear as glistening, refractile bodies at the disc margin, whereas buried drusen produce an elevated disc with blurred margins but no true swelling

Features favouring pseudopapilloedema over true papilloedema include an absent central cup, anomalous branching vessels, a lumpy disc contour and the lack of hyperaemia, exudates or nerve fibre layer oedema obscuring vessels
Most patients are asymptomatic, but drusen can cause progressive visual field defects, typically arcuate or nasal, and an enlarged blind spot
Ultrasonography demonstrates a highly reflective calcified body with acoustic shadowing and is a robust confirmatory test, as drusen autofluoresce and calcify
Enhanced-depth optical coherence tomography can directly visualise buried drusen and has become a preferred imaging modality
Management is largely observation with monitoring of visual fields, and rare complications such as choroidal neovascularisation or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy require specific attention
reference.pathophysiology: Optic disc drusen are calcified concretions that accumulate within the prelaminar optic nerve head, thought to arise from disturbed axonal metabolism and impaired axoplasmic transport in a congenitally crowded disc with a small scleral canal. Degenerating axonal mitochondria and extruded material undergo progressive calcification over time, which is why drusen are frequently buried in childhood and become more superficial and visible with age. The crowded, drusen-laden disc can mechanically compress adjacent nerve fibres, producing slowly progressive visual field defects, and the compromised vascular supply predisposes to ischaemic optic neuropathy and, rarely, peripapillary choroidal neovascularisation.
additionalDifferentials: True papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure
Optic neuritis or other inflammatory optic neuropathy
Infiltrative or compressive optic disc lesions
Optic disc oedema from malignant hypertension
Myelinated retinal nerve fibres and other congenital disc anomalies
additionalInvestigations: B-scan ultrasonography showing a calcified, highly reflective body with acoustic shadowing
Fundus autofluorescence, which highlights superficial drusen
Enhanced-depth or spectral-domain optical coherence tomography to visualise buried drusen
Automated perimetry to detect and monitor arcuate and nasal field defects
Fluorescein angiography to distinguish pseudopapilloedema (no true leakage) from genuine disc swelling
Neuroimaging when true papilloedema cannot be confidently excluded on clinical and ultrasound grounds
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss attributable to the drusen
Sudden visual loss suggesting anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Subretinal fluid or haemorrhage indicating peripapillary choroidal neovascularisation
Any doubt about coexisting true papilloedema, which mandates exclusion of raised intracranial pressure
reference.prognosis: Most patients retain good central vision throughout life, but slowly progressive peripheral field loss is common and irreversible; central vision is usually only threatened by uncommon complications such as ischaemic optic neuropathy or choroidal neovascularisation.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting pseudopapilloedema as true papilloedema and subjecting the patient to unnecessary lumbar puncture and imaging
Conversely, assuming disc elevation is drusen and missing coexisting raised intracranial pressure
Failing to monitor visual fields in an asymptomatic patient and overlooking progressive loss
Not recognising a treatable complication such as choroidal neovascularisation
Assuming absence of visible superficial drusen excludes buried drusen, which need ultrasound or OCT to detect
management: Recognise the drusen to avoid unnecessary neuroimaging and lumbar puncture, confirming pseudopapilloedema rather than true papilloedema with B-scan ultrasonography showing a calcified reflective body with acoustic shadowing
Observe and reassure asymptomatic patients, as there is no drusen-directed treatment
Perform periodic automated perimetry to detect and monitor the slowly progressive arcuate and nasal visual field defects
Manage associated anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and control vascular risk factors
Detect and treat peripapillary choroidal neovascularisation with anti-VEGF therapy
Arrange ongoing ophthalmology follow-up for surveillance of field and disc changes
